KEY MESSAGE 1...

Large scale ridging and strengthening Canadian high pressure
building eastward into northern New England through tomorrow
will provide us a stretch of dry and seasonably cool temperatures.
This is good news for those beginning their Thanksgiving travel
as there are no hazards to monitor. Temperatures will turn 
chilly tonight and tomorrow night with high confidence of early 
morning temperatures dropping into the 20s and even teens in the
higher terrain areas thanks to favorable radiational cooling.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

All eyes then turn to a developing coastal storm arriving on
Thanksgiving Day and continuing into Friday. The latest guidance
has come into better agreement with the start time of the 
precipitation. The latest cluster guidance show that the ECMWF 
and CMC ensembles seem to have a good handle on the strengthen 
of the upper level ridge overhead and suggest this will delay
the south to north arrival of precipitation until Thanksgiving
afternoon and evening for most of eastern NY and western New 
England. This means anyone planning to travel in the morning on 
Thanksgiving will likely have dry weather. 

Precipitation then arrives from south to north into areas 
mainly south of I-90 by 18 - 00 UTC Thursday before pushing 
north of I-90 by 21 - 03 UTC. The Canadian high over the 
Northeast ahead of our incoming coastal storm will provide us 
with a seasonably cool but very dry air mass before precip 
arrives. Low dew points in the teens and 20s will likely 
support wet-bulb cooling processes once precip begins. Easterly
winds in the low and mid-levels ahead of the incoming coast 
storm look quite robust with the u-componet of the wind and wind
speeds ranking within all-time highest values of the NAEFS 
model climatology which certainly is impressive. These easterly 
winds will quickly advect a marine modified air mass aloft 
supporting a mainly rain thermal profile for most areas. 
However, the very low sfc dew points and dry air in the low- 
levels should support wet-bulb cooling processes for elevations
at and above 1500 feet in the northern and eastern Catskills, 
southern Greens, Taconics, and western MA. Forecast soundings 
suggest an initial period of sleet and freezing rain as surface 
temperatures cool while the warm nose aloft increases. However, 
the impressive kinematics aloft should deepen the warm nose 
aloft to the point where wintry mix should transition to plain 
rain for most by Thursday evening. The exception continues to be
the higher peaks of the southern Adirondacks and spine of the 
southern Greens where freezing rain looks to linger into 
Thursday evening. Given increased confidence for an initial 
period of sleet/freezing rain in the higher terrain areas, the 
probabilities and footprint for minor impacts on the latest 
probabilistic Winter Weather Severity Index (WSSI-P) have 
increased with values ranging 10 to 30% Thursday afternoon into 
Thursday night in these areas. Locally higher values 40 - 60% 
are in the higher peaks of the southern Adirondacks where 
freezing rain lingers. This means there is a low to medium
chance travelers returning home from Thanksgiving festivities 
late Thursday P.M or evening in these areas will encounter
winter weather conditions and slippery travel. 

The strong wind anomalies associated with this maturing cyclone
will also advect a highly moisture rich plume from the 
Caribbean into the Northeast with integrated water vapor 
transport values ranking among the highest values within the 
NAEFS model climatology. The impressive incoming moisture 
combined with strong forcing for ascent and notable isentropic 
lift along the leading edge of the precipitation shield will 
produce a widespread soaking rainfall across eastern NY and 
western New England Thurs P.M into Thurs evening. Rain will 
likely fall moderate to even locally heavy at times as it 
arrives which can lead to slower travel for those returning 
home from Thanksgiving celebrations. Rainfall rates should 
decrease overnight as the dry slot advances northward. Given dry
antecedent conditions, flooding in not expected but cannot rule
out localized ponding of water in low-lying and poor drainage 
areas. The only river forecast point expected to reach flood 
stage is Poughkeepsie on the Hudson River during the Thursday 
early P.M high tide cycle. There is medium to high confidence in
widespread total rainfall values through 12 UTC Friday 
exceeding 0.75 inches with a 60 to 90% chance of values 
exceeding 1 inch along the east facing slopes of the eastern 
Greens, southern Adirondacks, and eastern Catskills due to 
upslope effects. Downsloping effects should lead to lower values
just west of the Taconics and in the western Adirondacks/Mohawk
Valley. Lingering showers continue into Friday and even Friday 
night as the parent cyclone and wrap around moisture moves
